title: Tricky lists for min
idea: TOOL: reason about ties, negatives, and single-item lists for min; mirror the max edge cases.

exercises.explanation: -10 is furthest below zero, so it is the smallest. Starting best at the first value handles negatives correctly.

exercises.prompt: Why can starting best at 0 give a WRONG smallest for [5, 8, 3]?
options: 0 is smaller than every value, so best would stay 0 — a value not in the list
0 is the smallest of the list
exercises.explanation: 0 beats every positive value for 'smallest', so best never updates to a real value. Start at nums[0].
All equal, so best stays 5. Same all-equal result as max — the value itself.
One item means that item is both the smallest and the biggest.

exercises.prompt: With ties for smallest (two 1s), the min loop still reports a single value, 1.
exercises.explanation: Min reports the smallest VALUE, not how many times it appears — mirror of max.

exercises.prompt: In [3, -2, 7, -9, -2], what does the min loop return?
exercises.explanation: best drops to -9, the smallest. Mixed signs are fine because best started at a real value.

exercises.prompt: Which lists have a smallest value of exactly 0? (pick all)
exercises.explanation: The first three bottom out at 0. The last has a -1, so its smallest is -1.

exercises.prompt: A savings balance can go negative (overdraft). For 'lowest balance', which start is safe?
exercises.explanation: Starting at the first real value handles negative balances. A fixed start like 0 can be wrong.

exercises.prompt: An all-positive list is the case that can expose a 'started at 0' bug in a MIN loop.
exercises.explanation: If every value is above 0, a best started at 0 never updates. Testing an all-positive list catches it (the mirror of max's all-negative test).
99 is the one dip below 100, so it is the smallest.
